mcqs.question: You run the same compiled binary three times from a terminal. What do the three resulting processes have in common?
options: They share a single address space so any of the three can crash the others
They share one PID because they came from the same binary
Only the first one is a real process; the rest are references to it
Nothing except the code they started from — each gets its own address space, registers, and PID
mcqs.explanation: A program is just bytes on disk; each run creates an independent process with its own memory, registers, and PID — running the same binary twice never means shared memory or a shared PID. Every invocation is a fully separate process, not a reference to a prior one.

mcqs.question: In a typical process address space layout, why do the heap and stack grow toward each other from opposite ends instead of each having a fixed, pre-allocated size?
options: So both can expand into the shared unused region without a hard size limit fixed at process start
Because the CPU can only address memory in one direction
It's a historical accident with no functional benefit
So the OS can tell them apart by which end of memory they occupy
mcqs.explanation: Growing from opposite ends toward a shared gap lets neither region need a fixed cap chosen in advance — whichever needs more space just grows further into the gap. It isn't about telling regions apart (the OS already knows via page table metadata) or a CPU addressing limitation.

mcqs.question: A function needs to return a large buffer that must stay valid after the function returns. Where should it be allocated, and why?
options: The stack, because stack allocation is faster than heap allocation
Either one — the OS reclaims stack memory lazily so it stays valid briefly after return
The stack, because only stack memory can be returned from a function in most languages
The heap, because stack frames are popped on return and any pointer into them becomes invalid
mcqs.explanation: A stack frame is destroyed the moment its function returns, so returning a pointer to stack memory is undefined behavior. Heap memory persists until explicitly freed (or garbage collected), which is exactly what data that must outlive its allocating function needs. Speed isn't the relevant criterion here.

mcqs.question: What do all threads within the same multi-threaded process share?
options: Nothing — each thread has a fully independent address space, like a separate process
Code, global data, and the heap — but each keeps its own stack and register set
Only the process ID, but each thread gets its own private heap
Only the stack — code and heap are duplicated per thread
mcqs.explanation: Threads in one process share the address space — code, global data, heap — because they're all execution paths within the same process. Each thread needs its own stack and registers precisely because each is independently executing instructions and making its own function calls.

mcqs.question: Process A sets a global variable to 42. Process B, running a copy of the same program, reads that same-named global variable. What does process B see?
options: 42, because global variables are shared across all instances of the same program
Whatever value process B's own copy of that variable holds — its memory is entirely separate from process A's
42, but only if both processes were started within the same second
An error, because reading a global variable across processes is not allowed by the language runtime
mcqs.explanation: Each process has its own private address space; process B's variable lives at a different physical memory location than process A's, regardless of matching names or timing. There's no language-level error either — the two variables are simply unrelated pieces of memory. Sharing state requires an explicit IPC mechanism.
